entries.meaning: Spend time somewhere or with someone without any particular purpose.
examples: I hung around for an hour and she never showed up.
Don't just hang around — grab a broom.
Kids hang around the 7-Eleven all summer.
He hung around the courthouse hoping for a quote.
She started hanging around with a rough crowd.
I don't hang around with them anymore.
That cough has hung around since January.

senses.head: Wait or linger with nothing to do
body: No object. The idea is aimlessness — time passing without a plan, often with a hint of impatience.
examples: I hung around for an hour and she never showed up.
Don't just hang around — grab a broom.

senses.head: Spend time in a place
body: With a place as the object. American English also says hang out at.
examples: Kids hang around the 7-Eleven all summer.
He hung around the courthouse hoping for a quote.

senses.head: hang around with — keep company with
body: About the people someone chooses, and usually a little disapproving when a parent says it.
examples: She started hanging around with a rough crowd.
I don't hang around with them anymore.

senses.head: Stay in place longer than expected
body: Of a thing, a smell, or a feeling that refuses to go away.
examples: That cough has hung around since January.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress lands on the particle — hang aROUND, not HANG around
entries.separable: no — the place or the person always follows the whole phrase. We hung around the parking lot, never ✗ we hung the parking lot around; with a pronoun, hang around them, never ✗ hang them around.
entries.transitive: either — it takes no object when it means "wait idly," and a place or (with with) a person otherwise
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and atelic, an activity that fills time (we hung around for an hour); sense 4 (that cough has hung around since January) shades toward a state, but it still takes the progressive freely.
entries.passive: no — the "wait" sense has no object at all, and the place and person senses are prepositional: ✗ the parking lot was hung around, ✗ she was hung around with.

entries.meaning: Hold yourself back from acting or moving forward, out of shyness or doubt.
examples: The new hires hung back while the veterans took the front row.
Don't hang back — ask her yourself.
He hung back at the door, unsure whether he was welcome.
Investors have hung back since the rates went up.
She hangs back in meetings and then emails her best idea an hour later.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hang BACK, never HANG back
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object to move; the particle sits right after the verb.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but about withholding action: the subject is doing something (declining to step forward), not being something.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no object to promote: ✗ the front row was hung back.

entries.meaning: Keep going through something difficult; almost always heard as hang in there.
examples: Hang in there — the results come back Friday.
She hung in through two rounds of layoffs.
If you can hang in for one more semester, the hard part is over.
He hung in there long after the rest of the team quit.
Tell him to hang in there; we're two votes short.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hang IN there, never HANG in there
entries.separable: n/a — no object; there in hang in there is not an object but part of the fixed phrase.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, durative: enduring over a stretch of time (she hung in through two rounds of layoffs).
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and there in hang in there is part of the fixed phrase, not an object: ✗ there was hung in.

entries.meaning: Wait, keep your grip, or depend on something, according to the sense.
examples: Hang on — I've got another call.
Hang on a second, that's not what the invoice says.
Hang on, this road gets rough.
She hung on until the rescue crew reached her.
The whole season hangs on Sunday's game.
Everything hung on whether the bank called the loan.
The students hung on his every word.

senses.head: Wait a moment
body: Informal and nearly always an imperative, on the phone or in person. Hold on is the interchangeable twin.
examples: Hang on — I've got another call.
Hang on a second, that's not what the invoice says.

senses.head: Keep a tight grip
body: Physical, and no object: what you grip goes after to.
examples: Hang on, this road gets rough.
She hung on until the rescue crew reached her.

senses.head: Depend on, be determined by
body: Here on is a preposition and the subject is usually a decision or an outcome.
examples: The whole season hangs on Sunday's game.
Everything hung on whether the bank called the loan.

senses.head: Listen with total attention
body: Fixed in hang on someone's every word.
examples: The students hung on his every word.

entries.pronunciation note: particle-stressed when it means wait or grip — hang ON; but verb-stressed when on is a true preposition, everything HANGS on the vote
entries.separable: no — nothing ever comes between hang and on. In the "depend" sense on is a preposition and keeps its object behind it: it hangs on the weather, ✗ it hangs the weather on; with a pronoun, it hangs on that, ✗ it hangs that on.
entries.transitive: either — no object in the "wait" and "grip" senses, an object after on in the "depend" sense
entries.verb type: action in the "wait" and "grip" senses — dynamic (hang on a second, hang on tight). Stative in the "depend" sense: it hangs on the weather is a relation, not an event.
entries.passive: no — the wait and grip senses take no object, and the stative on-phrase resists the prepositional passive: ✗ the weather is hung on.

entries.meaning: Keep something rather than give it up, sell it, or throw it away; also grip it tightly. Often written hang onto.
examples: Hang on to that receipt in case the drill quits.
They hung on to the house through the whole downturn.
I've hung on to his letters for thirty years.
Hang on to me — the ice is worse than it looks.
She hung on to her seat by fewer than three hundred votes.
It's ugly, but hang on to it; those parts are impossible to find.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle carries the stress — hang ON to it; the to reduces to /tə/
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Hang on to the receipt, ✗ hang the receipt on to; with a pronoun, hang on to it, ✗ hang it on to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when it means gripping (hang on to the railing); closer to a maintained state when it means keeping (we hung on to the deed for forty years).
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part prepositional passive is awkward at best: ✗ the railing was hung on to. Say the deed was kept instead.

entries.meaning: Spend time somewhere in a relaxed way; also, put washing outside to dry.
examples: We just hung out at her place and watched movies.
Who does he hang out with these days?
They've been hanging out together since middle school.
She hung the sheets out before the rain came.
He hangs out the laundry every Saturday.
Bring the towels in — I hung them out this morning.
The dog rode with his tongue hanging out.

senses.head: Spend time relaxing, socialize
body: Informal and very American. With people it takes with; with a place, at. No object follows the particle itself.
examples: We just hung out at her place and watched movies.
Who does he hang out with these days?
They've been hanging out together since middle school.

senses.head: Put washing outside to dry
body: Separable, and the split order is the everyday one.
examples: She hung the sheets out before the rain came.
He hangs out the laundry every Saturday.
Bring the towels in — I hung them out this morning.

senses.head: Lean or stick out
body: Of a tongue, a shirttail, or anything protruding.
examples: The dog rode with his tongue hanging out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hang OUT, and hang the wash OUT
entries.separable: yes in the laundry sense — hang out the wash or hang the wash out, and with a pronoun it must split: hang it out, never ✗ hang out it. The socializing sense takes no object at all, so nothing can come between.
entries.transitive: either — no object when it means "spend time," an object in the laundry sense
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: an activity in the socializing sense (we hung out at the diner), a telic act in the laundry sense (hang the wash out).
entries.passive: yes in the laundry sense — the sheets were hung out to dry, and the idiom he was left hung out to dry. No passive of the socializing sense: ✗ I was hung out with by them.

entries.meaning: Loom over someone as a threat or an unfinished worry. The noun hangover comes from it.
examples: The audit has hung over the department all year.
A possible strike hangs over the negotiations.
That conversation hung over dinner like weather.
For months the verdict hung over him and he barely slept.
There is a deadline hanging over us, so let's be quick.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed, because over here is a preposition with an object — HANGS over us, not hangs OVer us
entries.separable: no — what it hangs over always follows the preposition. The debt hangs over the family, ✗ the debt hangs the family over; with a pronoun, it hangs over us, ✗ it hangs us over.
entries.verb type: stative in effect — it names a condition that persists rather than an event (a lawsuit hangs over the company), though unlike most statives it takes the progressive: a deadline is hanging over her.
entries.passive: no — over is a preposition and the subject is the threat, not an agent: ✗ the family is hung over by the debt.

entries.meaning: Make sense as a whole, or stay united.
examples: His story doesn't hang together — the times are wrong.
The essay is well written, but it doesn't quite hang together.
Once we saw the receipts, the whole account hung together.
The band hung together for twenty years.
If we don't hang together, they'll pick us off one by one.

senses.head: Be coherent, make sense
body: Of a story, an argument, or an alibi whose parts fit each other.
examples: His story doesn't hang together — the times are wrong.
The essay is well written, but it doesn't quite hang together.
Once we saw the receipts, the whole account hung together.

senses.head: Stay united
body: Of people who stick with each other under pressure.
examples: The band hung together for twenty years.
If we don't hang together, they'll pick us off one by one.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress lands on the particle — hang toGETHer
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object to move.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.verb type: stative in sense 1 — coherence is a property of the story, not something it does (✗ the alibi is hanging together). Action (durative) in sense 2, of people staying united under pressure.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses: ✗ the story was hung together.

entries.meaning: End a phone call, put something on a hook, or retire from an activity.
examples: She said goodbye and hung up.
Don't hang up — I'm putting you on speaker.
He hung up on me twice.
Hang up your coat before you sit down.
He hung the wet towel up on the rail.
It's a nice jacket — hang it up instead of dropping it there.
After twenty seasons he finally hung up his skates.
The permit is hung up in the county office.
She's still hung up on her ex.

senses.head: End a phone call
body: Usually with no object; hang up on someone means ending it rudely, mid-conversation.
examples: She said goodbye and hung up.
Don't hang up — I'm putting you on speaker.
He hung up on me twice.

senses.head: Put on a hook or hanger
body: Separable, and the split order is at least as common.
examples: Hang up your coat before you sit down.
He hung the wet towel up on the rail.
It's a nice jacket — hang it up instead of dropping it there.

senses.head: Retire from a sport or a job
body: Fixed with the tool of the trade: hang up his cleats, her skates, the badge.
examples: After twenty seasons he finally hung up his skates.

senses.head: be hung up — be stuck or obsessed
body: Passive or adjectival. Hung up on something means unable to stop thinking about it; hung up alone means delayed.
examples: The permit is hung up in the county office.
She's still hung up on her ex.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hang it UP, never HANG it up
entries.русский: вешать трубку; вешать (на крючок); завершить карьеру
entries.separable: yes — hang up your coat or hang your coat up, and with a pronoun it must split: hang it up, never ✗ hang up it. The phone sense is often used with no object at all: he hung up on me.
entries.transitive: either — no object in the phone sense, an object in the others
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic in every live sense: ending a call, putting a coat on a hook, retiring the cleats. Sense 4 (be hung up on someone) is an adjectival state, not a verb use.
entries.passive: yes in the object senses — the coats were hung up by the door, his skates were hung up years ago. The fixed adjectival passive she's hung up on him is the ordinary form of sense 4.

entries.meaning: Go ahead and tackle something with energy; in older writing, attack.
examples: The keyboard's yours — have at it.
If you think you can fix the carburetor, have at it.
There's half a pie in the fridge. Have at it.
The knight cried "Have at thee!" and charged.
The puppy had at the couch cushions while we were out.

senses.head: Go ahead, help yourself, get to work on it
body: Nearly always the fixed have at it, offered as permission.
examples: The keyboard's yours — have at it.
If you think you can fix the carburetor, have at it.
There's half a pie in the fridge. Have at it.

senses.head: Attack
body: Archaic outside historical fiction and jokes about it.
examples: The knight cried "Have at thee!" and charged.
The puppy had at the couch cushions while we were out.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — HAVE at it; at reduces to /ət/, as prepositions do
entries.separable: no — the object always follows at. Have at the leftovers, ✗ have the leftovers at; with a pronoun, have at it, ✗ have it at.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and nearly frozen in the imperative have at it; the archaic "attack" sense is likewise a dynamic act.
entries.passive: no — at is a preposition and the phrase is fixed: ✗ the leftovers were had at, ✗ it was had at.

entries.meaning: Bring someone into your home — guests for the evening, or a worker for a job.
examples: We had the Kaminskis in for coffee.
They're having a plumber in on Thursday.
She had them in for an hour and sent them home with pie.
We haven't had anyone in since the baby was born.
If the wiring smells hot, have an electrician in today.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — have them IN, not HAVE them in
entries.separable: yes, and in practice it must split: have the neighbors in, have them in. ✗ Have in the neighbors is not idiomatic, and ✗ have in them is impossible.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic have, meaning "host," not stative possession, so the progressive is fine: we're having the neighbors in on Friday.
entries.passive: no — like other have idioms it refuses the passive: ✗ the neighbors were had in, ✗ a plumber was had in.

entries.meaning: Bear a lasting grudge against someone and look for chances to hurt them.
examples: That umpire has it in for our catcher.
She was sure the scheduler had it in for her.
Ever since the complaint, he's had it in for me.
I don't think the professor has it in for anyone; he grades everyone that hard.
You'd swear the weather has it in for this town.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on in, the particle in the middle — have it IN for me
entries.русский: иметь зуб на, точить зуб на
entries.separable: no — the phrase is frozen. The it never changes and never moves, and the person always follows for: he has it in for me, ✗ he has me in for it.
entries.transitive: yes — the person always follows for
entries.verb type: stative — a standing attitude, not an act, and it rejects the progressive: ✗ he is having it in for me.
entries.passive: no — the frozen it cannot move and stative have blocks the passive anyway: ✗ I am had it in for.

entries.meaning: Settle a quarrel by finally arguing it through face to face.
examples: They finally had it out in the parking lot.
I'm going to have it out with my landlord about the heat.
We had it out over the will and haven't spoken since.
Stop sulking and have it out with her.
After twenty years of hints, the sisters had it out.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — have it OUT with him
entries.separable: no — the it is frozen in place between the verb and the particle and can never be replaced by another noun: have it out with your brother, ✗ have the argument out. The person you argue with always follows with.
entries.transitive: yes — the fixed it, plus the person after with
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic, a single confrontation with an endpoint: we finally had it out in the parking lot.
entries.passive: no — the it is frozen and cannot be promoted: ✗ it was had out with him.
entries.see also: have it in for, hold out on

entries.meaning: Be wearing something; also, hold damaging information about someone.
examples: She had on the blue dress from the wedding.
He had nothing on but a towel.
That's my scarf — you had it on all day.
They've got nothing on him.
What exactly does the prosecutor have on your client?
I have a lot on this week.
You're having me on — she never said that.

senses.head: Be wearing
body: The ordinary way to describe what someone is dressed in at a moment. Unlike wear, it does not take the progressive: ✗ he is having on a coat.
examples: She had on the blue dress from the wedding.
He had nothing on but a towel.
That's my scarf — you had it on all day.

senses.head: Hold evidence against
body: Usually negative, and common in police and legal talk.
examples: They've got nothing on him.
What exactly does the prosecutor have on your client?

senses.head: Have scheduled
body: Of commitments; have a lot on is more British than American, where people say have a lot going on.
examples: I have a lot on this week.

senses.head: Tease, fool
body: British. An American would say pull someone's leg or mess with someone.
examples: You're having me on — she never said that.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — she had a red coat ON
entries.русский: быть одетым в, носить; иметь компромат на; разыгрывать (брит.)
entries.separable: yes — he had on a heavy coat or he had a heavy coat on, and with a pronoun it must split: he had it on, never ✗ he had on it.
entries.verb type: stative — "be wearing" is a state, and the entry notes it refuses the progressive: ✗ he is having on a coat. Sense 2 (what they have on him) is equally stative; only the British "tease" sense is dynamic.
entries.passive: no — this is the classic stative have that learners try to passivize: ✗ a heavy coat was had on by him, ✗ nothing is had on me. Use wear or hold if you need a passive.

entries.meaning: Invite someone to your home. The American default; British English says have someone round.
examples: We're having my parents over on Sunday.
Have them over — the grill is already going.
She had the whole team over after the game.
They haven't had us over once since they moved.
Why don't you have him over and just talk it through?
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — have them Over, not HAVE them over
entries.separable: yes, and it must split in practice: have the Nguyens over, have them over. ✗ Have over the Nguyens is not idiomatic and ✗ have over them is impossible.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic have, meaning "host": we're having the Nguyens over Saturday is perfectly natural in the progressive.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the Nguyens were had over; English simply has no passive for this idiom. Say they were invited over.

entries.meaning: Learn a piece of news; in a warning, be scolded for something.
examples: I heard about the layoffs from a friend in payroll.
Have you heard about the new bridge?
We only heard about it after the funeral.
If your mother finds that dent, you'll hear about it.
The mayor is going to hear about this at the next meeting.

senses.head: Get news of
body: The everyday sense: information reaches you, usually secondhand.
examples: I heard about the layoffs from a friend in payroll.
Have you heard about the new bridge?
We only heard about it after the funeral.

senses.head: Be scolded, face the consequences
body: Always in the future and always a threat: you'll hear about it.
examples: If your mother finds that dent, you'll hear about it.
The mayor is going to hear about this at the next meeting.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — HEARD about it; the preposition stays weak
entries.русский: узнавать о, слышать о; получить нагоняй
entries.separable: no — the news always follows about. I heard about the fire, ✗ I heard the fire about; with a pronoun, I heard about it, ✗ I heard it about.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an achievement: news reaches you at a moment (I heard about the fire last night), though the progressive works for repeated report: we've been hearing about it all week.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is awkward: ✗ the fire was heard about, and the threat sense has none at all: ✗ it will be heard about.

entries.meaning: Receive a letter, a call, or any word from someone. Note that it is about being contacted, not about literally hearing.
examples: I haven't heard from my brother since Christmas.
You'll hear from our lawyer.
We heard from the school that he'd missed three days.
Great to hear from you — it's been years.
If you don't hear from us by Friday, the position went to someone else.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — HEAR from her; from reduces to /frəm/
entries.separable: no — the person always follows from. I heard from my sister, ✗ I heard my sister from; with a pronoun, we heard from them, ✗ we heard them from.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: being contacted is an event, not a state (we heard from her on Tuesday).
entries.passive: restricted — natural only in the fixed negative: she hasn't been heard from since Tuesday. Elsewhere it fails: ✗ I was heard from by my boss.

entries.meaning: Know that someone or something exists; in the negative, refuse to allow something.
examples: I've never heard of her.
Everybody in Ohio has heard of that diner.
Had you heard of the disease before the diagnosis?
I offered to pay and she wouldn't hear of it.
His father would not hear of art school.

senses.head: Know of the existence of
body: Almost always in the perfect and very often negative. It says you know the name, not the person.
examples: I've never heard of her.
Everybody in Ohio has heard of that diner.
Had you heard of the disease before the diagnosis?

senses.head: won't hear of it — refuse to allow
body: Fixed and always negative. It refuses even to discuss the thing.
examples: I offered to pay and she wouldn't hear of it.
His father would not hear of art school.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — never HEARD of him; of reduces to /əv/
entries.русский: слышать о (о существовании); и слышать не хотеть
entries.separable: no — the object always follows of. I've heard of that band, ✗ I've heard that band of; with a pronoun, never heard of it, ✗ never heard it of.
entries.verb type: stative in effect — the perfect I've heard of them reports a state of knowledge, not an act of hearing; won't hear of it is a standing refusal.
entries.passive: restricted — fine in the negative or with a modifier: a writer nobody had ever heard of. Otherwise it fails: ✗ that band was heard of by me.

entries.meaning: Listen to someone's whole explanation without cutting them off.
examples: Just hear me out before you say no.
The board heard the whistleblower out for two hours.
She never hears anyone out; she's already arguing.
Hear him out — the plan is better than it sounds.
They wouldn't even hear out the tenants who showed up.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hear me OUT, never HEAR me out
entries.separable: yes — hear out the witness or hear the witness out, and with a pronoun it must split: hear me out, never ✗ hear out me.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — and the object is a person
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic: listening to a person all the way through, with a clear endpoint.
entries.passive: yes — the witness was heard out before the vote, she deserves to be heard out.

entries.meaning: Put something where nobody will find it, or take yourself somewhere nobody will.
examples: She hid the letters away in a shoebox.
He hides away a little cash every payday.
The deed was in the attic — someone had hidden it away decades ago.
He hides away in the cabin every winter to write.
You can't hide away from this forever.

senses.head: Conceal something
body: Separable, with a strong sense of squirreling the thing away for a long time.
examples: She hid the letters away in a shoebox.
He hides away a little cash every payday.
The deed was in the attic — someone had hidden it away decades ago.

senses.head: Go somewhere out of sight
body: No object, often reflexive in feeling: withdrawing from people.
examples: He hides away in the cabin every winter to write.
You can't hide away from this forever.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hide it aWAY
entries.separable: yes — hide away the cash or hide the cash away, and with a pronoun it must split: hide it away, never ✗ hide away it. With no object it simply means going into hiding.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you hide a thing, none when you hide yourself
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: concealing a thing (hide the cash away) and withdrawing yourself (he hid away in a cabin).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the cash had been hidden away behind a wall. No passive of the intransitive sense: ✗ the cabin was hidden away in (in that reading).

entries.meaning: Use something as a shield so you don't have to answer for yourself.
examples: He hides behind company policy every time.
Stop hiding behind your lawyer and say it yourself.
The agency hid behind an exemption to withhold the emails.
She hides behind humor whenever the subject gets serious.
It's a rule, not a wall — don't hide behind it.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — HIDE behind a rule; behind is a preposition with its own object
entries.separable: no — the excuse always follows behind. He hides behind the rules, ✗ he hides the rules behind; with a pronoun, hide behind it, ✗ hide it behind.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in form, though it describes a sustained stance: he keeps hiding behind the rules.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive does not work here: ✗ the rules are hidden behind by managers.

entries.meaning: Stay somewhere out of sight to avoid being found, especially by the police.
examples: The pair hid out in a motel outside Reno.
He's been hiding out at his cousin's since the indictment.
We hid out in the basement until the storm passed.
She hides out in the library during finals week.
You can't hide out here forever; somebody will talk.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hide OUT, never HIDE out
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object to move; the place goes in a separate phrase with in or at.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: staying out of sight over a stretch of time.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the place sits in a separate in/at phrase: ✗ the motel was hidden out in.

entries.meaning: Retaliate, with a punch or with words.
examples: He never hit back, not once.
The senator hit back at the ad within an hour.
If you hit back, you both get suspended.
The company hit back with a lawsuit of its own.
She hit back hard in the second debate.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hit BACK, never HIT back
entries.separable: n/a — it takes no object; the target goes after at, as in hit back at his critics.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes a direct object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic: a single act of retaliation, with a punch or a statement.
entries.passive: no — there is no direct object, and the at-phrase resists promotion: ✗ his critics were hit back at.

entries.meaning: Get along easily and immediately with someone you have just met.
examples: They hit it off the minute they met.
I hit it off with her roommate right away.
The two of them didn't exactly hit it off.
We hit it off over a shared hatred of the coffee.
He's shy, but he hits it off with anyone who likes trains.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hit it OFF
entries.separable: no — the it is frozen between the verb and the particle and can never be swapped for a noun: they hit it off, ✗ they hit the friendship off. The other person follows with.
entries.transitive: yes — the fixed it, plus an optional person after with
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: it names the moment a rapport starts (they hit it off right away), not the friendship that follows.
entries.passive: no — the frozen it cannot become a subject: ✗ it was hit off with her.

entries.meaning: Come upon an idea by luck, or make a romantic advance. Hit upon is the slightly more formal variant of the first sense only.
examples: She hit on the answer in the shower.
They hit upon a way to cool the servers for half the cost.
We hit on it by accident.
Some guy hit on her at the bar.
He got fired for hitting on an intern.

senses.head: Suddenly think of
body: Neutral in register, and interchangeable with hit upon. The idea arrives rather than being worked out.
examples: She hit on the answer in the shower.
They hit upon a way to cool the servers for half the cost.
We hit on it by accident.

senses.head: Make a pass at someone
body: Informal and American, always about unwanted or at least uninvited flirting. Never hit upon in this sense.
examples: Some guy hit on her at the bar.
He got fired for hitting on an intern.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — he HIT on the idea; on is a preposition here, not a stressed particle
entries.separable: no — the object always follows on. She hit on a solution, ✗ she hit a solution on; with a pronoun, he hit on her, ✗ he hit her on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: an achievement in sense 1 (the idea arrives) and an activity in sense 2 (making a pass).
entries.passive: yes — she got hit on twice before last call; the idea sense passivizes in a more formal register: the solution was hit upon by accident.

entries.meaning: Attack someone verbally, especially in a public statement.
examples: The minister hit out at the media coverage.
Campaigners hit out over the delay in funding.
He hit out at what he called a stitch-up.
The union hit out at the pay offer as insulting.
An American paper would say the senator lashed out rather than hit out.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hit OUT at the report
entries.separable: n/a — it takes no direct object; the target follows at: hit out at the ruling, ✗ hit the ruling out.
entries.transitive: no — the target goes after at
entries.register: British — standard in British newspapers; Americans write lash out at or hit back at
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic: a single public attack, usually reported as one event.
entries.passive: no — there is no direct object, and the at-phrase will not passivize: ✗ the ruling was hit out at.

entries.meaning: Ask someone for money or a favor; also, go to a place.
examples: He hit me up for forty bucks.
Hit up your cousin — he's got a truck.
She hit the whole department up for raffle tickets.
Let's hit up that taco place after work.
We hit up three yard sales before noon.

senses.head: Ask someone for something
body: What you are asking for follows for. Slightly cheeky, never used in writing to a stranger.
examples: He hit me up for forty bucks.
Hit up your cousin — he's got a truck.
She hit the whole department up for raffle tickets.

senses.head: Go to a place
body: American and casual, mostly about food, bars, and errands.
examples: Let's hit up that taco place after work.
We hit up three yard sales before noon.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hit him UP for a loan
entries.separable: yes — hit up your brother for a loan or hit your brother up for a loan, and with a pronoun it must split: hit him up, never ✗ hit up him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: asking someone for something, or going to a place.
entries.passive: yes, though informal, and the get-passive is the usual form: I got hit up for money twice today; he was hit up for a loan.

entries.meaning: Resent someone for something they did, and let it color how you treat them.
examples: I asked for a raise at a bad moment, and she held it against me for a year.
Nobody holds the fumble against him.
He was nineteen; don't hold it against him now.
The bank held the late payment against our application.
If I say no, will you hold it against me?
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — don't HOLD it against me; against is a preposition and stays weak
entries.русский: ставить в вину, держать зло за
entries.separable: yes, and it must split — the thing resented sits between the verb and against, and the person always follows: hold the mistake against him, ✗ hold against him the mistake. With a pronoun, don't hold it against me, ✗ don't hold against me it.
entries.transitive: yes — two objects, one before against and one after
entries.verb type: stative in effect — a lasting resentment rather than an act, though the progressive is common in the denial: I'm not holding it against you.
entries.passive: restricted — the resented thing can be the subject (that shouldn't be held against her), but the person never can: ✗ he was held the mistake against.
entries.see also: have it in for, hold out on

entries.meaning: Restrain someone or something, keep something to yourself, or hesitate.
examples: Two officers held back the crowd.
She held the dog back by the collar.
The levee held them back for six hours.
He was holding back the most useful part of the story.
The insurer held ten percent back until the inspection.
Tell me all of it — don't hold anything back.
She couldn't hold back the tears.
He held back a laugh and nodded.
Buyers are holding back until rates fall.
He was held back a year in elementary school.

senses.head: Physically restrain
body: Separable. Of a crowd, a dog, a door, or floodwater.
examples: Two officers held back the crowd.
She held the dog back by the collar.
The levee held them back for six hours.

senses.head: Keep information or money to yourself
body: Separable, and the split order is common with short objects.
examples: He was holding back the most useful part of the story.
The insurer held ten percent back until the inspection.
Tell me all of it — don't hold anything back.

senses.head: Restrain your feelings
body: Chiefly of tears, laughter, and anger.
examples: She couldn't hold back the tears.
He held back a laugh and nodded.

senses.head: Hesitate, not commit
body: No object, and close to hang back.
examples: Buyers are holding back until rates fall.

senses.head: Keep a student from advancing a grade
body: American school usage, usually passive.
examples: He was held back a year in elementary school.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold them BACK, never HOLD them back
entries.русский: сдерживать; утаивать; мяться; оставлять на второй год
entries.separable: yes — hold back the crowd or hold the crowd back, and with a pronoun it must split: hold them back, never ✗ hold back them. With no object it means hesitating.
entries.transitive: either — an object in most senses, none when it means "hesitate"
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: restraining, withholding, choking back tears, or hesitating.
entries.passive: yes — the crowd was held back by barricades, she was held back a grade, the report was held back for a week. No passive of the "hesitate" sense, which has no object.
entries.see also: hang back, keep back, hold out

entries.meaning: Keep something in place or at a low level; also, manage to keep a job.
examples: It took three of them to hold him down for the shot.
Hold down the corner of the tarp while I stake it.
The chain holds prices down by buying in bulk.
Guys, hold it down — the baby's asleep.
He hasn't held down a job since the accident.
She held down two jobs the whole time she was in school.
Hold down the fort — I'll be back by three.

senses.head: Keep in place by force
body: Separable and literal.
examples: It took three of them to hold him down for the shot.
Hold down the corner of the tarp while I stake it.

senses.head: Keep low
body: Of prices, noise, inflation, a heart rate. Hold it down as an imperative means "be quieter."
examples: The chain holds prices down by buying in bulk.
Guys, hold it down — the baby's asleep.

senses.head: Keep a job
body: Fixed in hold down a job, usually about whether someone can.
examples: He hasn't held down a job since the accident.
She held down two jobs the whole time she was in school.

senses.head: Cover for someone
body: Fixed in hold down the fort: keep things running while others are away.
examples: Hold down the fort — I'll be back by three.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold it DOWN
entries.separable: yes — hold down the costs or hold the costs down, and with a pronoun it must split: hold it down, never ✗ hold down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: keeping something pinned, keeping a level low, or managing to stay employed.
entries.passive: yes in the literal and "keep low" senses — his arms were held down, costs were held down for a decade. Awkward in the job idiom: ✗ a job was held down by him.

entries.meaning: Talk at length and with obvious self-satisfaction.
examples: He held forth on the decline of the newspaper for forty minutes.
She held forth about zoning to anyone who would listen.
Uncle Ray was already holding forth when we arrived.
The professor held forth while the students quietly packed their bags.
Give him a glass of wine and he'll hold forth until midnight.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold FORTH
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object; the subject spoken about follows on or about.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.register: formal — bookish, and usually said with a raised eyebrow
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: talking at length is an activity, and the progressive suits it: he was holding forth about zoning again.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; the topic sits in an on/about phrase: ✗ zoning was held forth on.

entries.meaning: Delay doing something, or keep something from reaching you.
examples: Let's hold off until the inspection comes back.
We held off on buying until spring.
The defense held off Kansas City for one more drive.
She held the reporters off with a two-line statement.
Zinc won't cure a cold, but you feel like it's holding it off.
The rain held off until the last inning.

senses.head: Wait, postpone acting
body: No object; what is postponed follows on.
examples: Let's hold off until the inspection comes back.
We held off on buying until spring.

senses.head: Keep at bay
body: Separable. Of attackers, reporters, a rival team, a cold.
examples: The defense held off Kansas City for one more drive.
She held the reporters off with a two-line statement.
Zinc won't cure a cold, but you feel like it's holding it off.

senses.head: Fail to arrive — of weather
body: No object, always of rain or snow.
examples: The rain held off until the last inning.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold them OFF
entries.separable: yes when it has an object — hold off the attackers or hold the attackers off, and with a pronoun it must split: hold them off, never ✗ hold off them. In the "wait" sense there is no object and nothing can come between.
entries.transitive: either — no object when it means "wait," an object when it means "keep at bay"
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: postponing, repelling, or (of weather) failing to arrive.
entries.passive: yes in the "keep at bay" sense — the reporters were held off for an hour. No passive of the "wait" or weather senses: ✗ the rain was held off.
entries.see also: hold out, keep off, hold up

entries.meaning: Wait, or keep your grip and endure.
examples: Hold on, I'll transfer you.
Hold on — you signed it without reading it?
Hold on tight, this bus driver is in a mood.
He held on until his fingers gave out.
The company held on for two more quarters.
Hold on a little longer — help is twenty minutes out.

senses.head: Wait a moment
body: Usually an imperative, and the standard thing to say on the phone.
examples: Hold on, I'll transfer you.
Hold on — you signed it without reading it?

senses.head: Keep a grip
body: Physical, no object.
examples: Hold on tight, this bus driver is in a mood.
He held on until his fingers gave out.

senses.head: Endure, keep going
body: Of people and of situations that are barely lasting.
examples: The company held on for two more quarters.
Hold on a little longer — help is twenty minutes out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold ON
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object. What you grip follows to, which turns it into the three-part hold on to.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes a direct object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: waiting, gripping, or enduring, all of them things the subject does over time.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; what you grip goes after to: ✗ the railing was held on.
entries.see also: hold on to, hang on, hold out

entries.meaning: Grip something, or keep it instead of letting it go. Often written hold onto.
examples: Hold on to the railing — those stairs are iced.
They held on to the farm through two bad years.
She's held on to every letter he sent.
Hold on to your ticket stub; you'll need it to get back in.
It's worth more than you think — hold on to it.
He held on to a one-point lead with eight seconds left.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle carries the stress — hold ON to it; to reduces to /tə/
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Hold on to the railing, ✗ hold the railing on to; with a pronoun, hold on to it, ✗ hold it on to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when it means gripping (hold on to the rail), closer to a maintained state when it means keeping (they held on to the house).
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part passive is clumsy: ✗ the railing was held on to. Use kept for the retention sense.
entries.see also: hang on to, hold on, keep to

entries.meaning: Extend something toward someone; resist; or last.
examples: He held out his hand and I shook it.
She held the photograph out so I could see it.
Doctors hold out little hope of a full recovery.
Here's the badge — hold it out where the guard can see it.
The strikers held out for eleven weeks.
The last two holdouts held out until the deadline passed.
If the water holds out, we can stay another day.
My knee held out through the whole hike.

senses.head: Extend, offer
body: Separable. Of a hand, a cup, a bribe, a hope.
examples: He held out his hand and I shook it.
She held the photograph out so I could see it.
Doctors hold out little hope of a full recovery.
Here's the badge — hold it out where the guard can see it.

senses.head: Resist, refuse to give in
body: No object. Of a garrison, a strike, a negotiator.
examples: The strikers held out for eleven weeks.
The last two holdouts held out until the deadline passed.

senses.head: Last, be enough
body: No object. Of supplies, money, weather, or an engine.
examples: If the water holds out, we can stay another day.
My knee held out through the whole hike.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold it OUT
entries.русский: протягивать; держаться, не сдаваться; хватать (о запасах)
entries.separable: yes in the "extend" sense — hold out your hand or hold your hand out, and with a pronoun it must split: hold it out, never ✗ hold out it. The "resist" and "last" senses take no object, so nothing can come between.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you extend something, none when you resist or last
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: extending something, resisting, or lasting until supplies run out.
entries.passive: yes in the "extend/offer" sense — a deal was held out to the strikers, little hope is held out for a settlement. No passive of the "resist" or "last" senses, which take no object.
entries.see also: hold out for, hold out on, hold on

entries.meaning: Refuse to settle until you get the thing you want.
examples: He's holding out for a signing bonus.
The union held out for full pension protection.
Don't take the first offer — hold out for the corner office.
She held out for a written apology and eventually got one.
The car's fine, but the color is wrong, so I'm holding out for another.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress — hold OUT for more; for reduces to /fər/
entries.русский: добиваться, настаивать на, не соглашаться меньше чем на
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Hold out for a better offer, ✗ hold a better offer out for; with a pronoun, hold out for it, ✗ hold it out for.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: refusing to settle is something the subject keeps doing.
entries.passive: no — the three-part prepositional passive fails: ✗ a better offer was held out for.

entries.meaning: Keep something back from someone who has a right to know it or share it.
examples: You've been holding out on me — when did you get engaged?
The witness was clearly holding out on the detectives.
Don't hold out on your own lawyer.
He held out on his partners for months about the second offer.
She's got the good coffee somewhere; she's holding out on us.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress — hold OUT on me
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Hold out on your partner, ✗ hold your partner out on; with a pronoun, don't hold out on me, ✗ don't hold me out on.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — and the object is a person
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: withholding something from someone over a stretch of time.
entries.passive: no — ✗ I was held out on; the idiom has no usable passive. Say he kept it from me.
entries.see also: hold out, hold back, keep from

entries.meaning: Postpone something to a later date, keep it running longer, or use it as a threat.
examples: The council held the rezoning over until June.
Hold over the vote — half the board is out sick.
It was on the agenda twice and they held it over both times.
The exhibit was held over for another month.
Two of the appointees were held over into the new administration.
He held that favor over me for years.

senses.head: Postpone to a later meeting
body: Separable, and common in the language of boards and committees.
examples: The council held the rezoning over until June.
Hold over the vote — half the board is out sick.
It was on the agenda twice and they held it over both times.

senses.head: Keep on longer than planned
body: Of a show, an exhibit, or an employee kept past a term.
examples: The exhibit was held over for another month.
Two of the appointees were held over into the new administration.

senses.head: hold something over someone — use as leverage
body: The threat sits between the verb and over.
examples: He held that favor over me for years.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold it Over
entries.separable: yes — hold over the vote or hold the vote over, and with a pronoun it must split: hold it over, never ✗ hold over it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and telic in all three senses: postponing, extending a run, or dangling a threat.
entries.passive: yes — the vote was held over until March, the show was held over another week, it was held over him for years.
entries.see also: hold up, hang over, lay over

entries.meaning: Stay in one piece, or keep something in one piece.
examples: The old barn held together through the whole storm.
The coalition held together just long enough to pass the budget.
Her mother held the family together after the fire.
Two screws and a prayer are holding it together.
She held it together until the last guest left.

senses.head: Stay intact
body: No object. Of an object, a coalition, a marriage, an argument.
examples: The old barn held together through the whole storm.
The coalition held together just long enough to pass the budget.

senses.head: Keep something united
body: Separable.
examples: Her mother held the family together after the fire.
Two screws and a prayer are holding it together.

senses.head: hold it together — stay composed
body: Fixed with it, about keeping your emotions in check.
examples: She held it together until the last guest left.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold it toGETHer
entries.separable: yes when it has an object — hold the team together or hold together the team, and with a pronoun it must split: hold it together, never ✗ hold together it. With no object it means staying intact.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you keep something united, none when it stays intact by itself
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and transitive when someone keeps a thing united; the objectless sense (the coalition held together) is a durative process verging on a state.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the coalition was held together by one man. No passive of the intransitive sense, nor of the fixed hold it together: ✗ it was held together by her in that reading.

entries.meaning: Delay something, rob it at gunpoint, support it, or stay sound under pressure.
examples: An accident held up traffic for an hour.
The permit held the whole project up six months.
Sorry — a call held me up.
Two men held up the gas station on Third.
They held the armored car up in broad daylight.
His alibi didn't hold up under questioning.
The paint has held up remarkably well.
Do the numbers hold up if you exclude last quarter?
Four bolts hold up the entire shelf.
The district holds her up as a model teacher.

senses.head: Delay
body: Separable and very common. The noun holdup means the delay.
examples: An accident held up traffic for an hour.
The permit held the whole project up six months.
Sorry — a call held me up.

senses.head: Rob at gunpoint
body: Separable. The noun holdup also means the robbery.
examples: Two men held up the gas station on Third.
They held the armored car up in broad daylight.

senses.head: Stay sound, remain valid
body: No object. Of a theory, an alibi, a knee, a pair of boots.
examples: His alibi didn't hold up under questioning.
The paint has held up remarkably well.
Do the numbers hold up if you exclude last quarter?

senses.head: Support, keep from falling
body: Separable and literal.
examples: Four bolts hold up the entire shelf.

senses.head: hold someone up as — present as an example
body: The person sits between the verb and up.
examples: The district holds her up as a model teacher.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — hold it UP, never HOLD it up
entries.separable: yes — hold up traffic or hold traffic up, and with a pronoun it must split: hold it up, never ✗ hold up it. The "stay valid" sense takes no object.
entries.transitive: either — an object in the delay, robbery, and support senses; none when something stays valid
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: delaying, robbing, supporting, or (objectless) standing up to scrutiny.
entries.passive: yes — traffic was held up for an hour, the bank was held up in broad daylight, she was held up as a model. No passive of the "stay valid" sense: ✗ the alibi was held up, which reads only as "delayed."
entries.see also: hold off, hold down, hang up

entries.meaning: Approve of something, in the sense of being willing to go along with it.
examples: She doesn't hold with all this online banking.
My grandfather never held with doctors.
They don't hold with working on Sundays.
I don't hold with the idea that children should be seen and not heard.
He'd say he doesn't hold with gossip, and then repeat every word of it.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — I don't HOLD with that; with is a preposition and stays weak
entries.separable: no — the object always follows with. He doesn't hold with such things, ✗ he doesn't hold such things with; with a pronoun, I don't hold with it, ✗ I don't hold it with.
entries.register: rare — dated, and almost always in the negative
entries.verb type: stative — an attitude of approval, not an act, and it rejects the progressive: ✗ I am not holding with it.
entries.passive: no — a stative prepositional verb, so the passive is out: ✗ such things aren't held with.

entries.meaning: Persist at something without letting up.
examples: Keep at it — you're closer than you think.
She kept at the scales for an hour every morning.
He kept at the loose screw until the whole shelf came down.
The coach kept them at it until dark.
If you keep at the language for a year, you'll surprise yourself.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — KEEP at it; at reduces to /ət/
entries.русский: упорно продолжать, не бросать; заставлять продолжать
entries.separable: no — the task always follows at. Keep at the exercises, ✗ keep the exercises at; with a pronoun, keep at it, ✗ keep it at. When a person is kept at a task, the person goes between: keep him at it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: persisting at a task, or making someone persist at one.
entries.passive: restricted — a person kept at a task can be the subject (they were kept at it until dark), but the task itself cannot: ✗ the exercises were kept at.

entries.meaning: Stay at a distance, or make something stay at a distance.
examples: Keep away from the edge.
He's been told to keep away from the property.
Citronella keeps the mosquitoes away.
A porch light keeps away most trouble.
The dog barks at strangers, which keeps them away.

senses.head: Stay at a distance
body: No object; what you avoid follows from.
examples: Keep away from the edge.
He's been told to keep away from the property.

senses.head: Make something stay at a distance
body: Separable, and the split order is the everyday one.
examples: Citronella keeps the mosquitoes away.
A porch light keeps away most trouble.
The dog barks at strangers, which keeps them away.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep them aWAY
entries.separable: yes — keep away the flies or keep the flies away, and with a pronoun it must split: keep them away, never ✗ keep away them. With no object it is a warning to stay back.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you keep something at a distance, none when you stay away yourself
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: staying at a distance yourself, or making something stay at one.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the flies were kept away with a fan, children were kept away from the site. No passive of the objectless warning keep away!

entries.meaning: Hold something in reserve, hide it, or keep people at a distance.
examples: He kept back the part about the second loan.
She wasn't lying, but she kept a good deal back.
Whatever you know, don't keep it back now.
We keep back ten percent for repairs.
Keep a couple of jars back for winter.
Keep back — there's glass everywhere.

senses.head: Withhold information
body: Separable, and close to hold back.
examples: He kept back the part about the second loan.
She wasn't lying, but she kept a good deal back.
Whatever you know, don't keep it back now.

senses.head: Hold in reserve
body: Of money, seed, supplies.
examples: We keep back ten percent for repairs.
Keep a couple of jars back for winter.

senses.head: Stay or hold at a distance
body: Often an imperative with no object.
examples: Keep back — there's glass everywhere.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep it BACK
entries.separable: yes — keep back part of the payment or keep part of the payment back, and with a pronoun it must split: keep it back, never ✗ keep back it. As a shouted warning it takes no object: keep back!
entries.transitive: either — an object in most uses, none in the warning keep back!
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: withholding, reserving, or holding people at a distance.
entries.passive: yes — part of the payment was kept back, the crowd was kept back behind the tape. No passive of the shouted keep back!, which has no object.

entries.meaning: Keep something at a low level, keep food in your stomach, or keep a people subjugated.
examples: Keep the noise down after ten.
Buying in bulk keeps down the cost per meal.
The music's too loud — keep it down.
He couldn't keep anything down for two days.
She managed to keep down some broth.
The system was designed to keep people down.
Keep down until the truck passes.

senses.head: Keep at a low level
body: Separable. Of noise, prices, weight, a heart rate.
examples: Keep the noise down after ten.
Buying in bulk keeps down the cost per meal.
The music's too loud — keep it down.

senses.head: Not vomit
body: Of food and medicine, usually in the negative.
examples: He couldn't keep anything down for two days.
She managed to keep down some broth.

senses.head: Oppress, prevent from rising
body: Of a group or a class of people.
examples: The system was designed to keep people down.

senses.head: Stay low
body: No object, usually an imperative.
examples: Keep down until the truck passes.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep it DOWN
entries.separable: yes — keep down the noise or keep the noise down, and with a pronoun it must split: keep it down, never ✗ keep down it.
entries.transitive: either — usually an object; none when it means staying low physically
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: suppressing a level, holding food in, oppressing a group, or staying low.
entries.passive: yes in the "keep low" and "oppress" senses — prices were kept down by the freeze, the region was kept down for generations. Awkward in the food sense: ✗ the medicine wasn't kept down by her.

entries.meaning: Stop someone from doing something, hide something from them, or stop yourself.
examples: Nothing was going to keep her from finishing.
A cracked rib kept him from playing.
They kept the diagnosis from their kids for a month.
Don't keep anything from me.
I could hardly keep from laughing.
He kept from saying what he actually thought.

senses.head: Prevent from doing
body: The person goes between the verb and from, and the action follows in -ing.
examples: Nothing was going to keep her from finishing.
A cracked rib kept him from playing.

senses.head: Withhold from someone
body: The thing goes between the verb and from, and the person follows.
examples: They kept the diagnosis from their kids for a month.
Don't keep anything from me.

senses.head: Refrain, stop yourself
body: No middle object; the action follows in -ing.
examples: I could hardly keep from laughing.
He kept from saying what he actually thought.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — KEEP him from going; from reduces to /frəm/
entries.русский: удерживать от; скрывать от; удерживаться от
entries.separable: yes in the "prevent" and "withhold" senses, and there it must split — the person or thing being kept sits between the verb and from: keep him from leaving, ✗ keep from him leaving; with a pronoun, keep her from it, ✗ keep from her it. When it means "refrain," there is no middle object at all: keep from laughing.
entries.transitive: either — an object before from in the "prevent" and "withhold" senses, none in "refrain"
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: preventing, withholding, or restraining yourself.
entries.passive: yes in the "prevent" and "withhold" senses — she was kept from seeing her kids, the diagnosis was kept from the family. No passive of the "refrain" sense, which has no middle object.

entries.meaning: Not let someone or something out; also, hold feelings inside.
examples: We kept the kids in all weekend with the smoke.
The storm windows keep in the heat.
The cat wants out, but keep him in until the vet call.
The teacher kept him in at recess.
He keeps everything in and then explodes in April.
She keeps in with the people who approve the budget.

senses.head: Not let out
body: Separable. Of children, animals, heat, air.
examples: We kept the kids in all weekend with the smoke.
The storm windows keep in the heat.
The cat wants out, but keep him in until the vet call.

senses.head: Detain a student after class
body: American school usage.
examples: The teacher kept him in at recess.

senses.head: Hold feelings inside
body: Usually with it or everything.
examples: He keeps everything in and then explodes in April.

senses.head: keep in with — stay on good terms
body: British; an American would say stay on someone's good side.
examples: She keeps in with the people who approve the budget.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep it IN
entries.русский: не выпускать, держать дома; оставлять после уроков; сдерживать (чувства)
entries.separable: yes — keep in the heat or keep the heat in, and with a pronoun it must split: keep them in, never ✗ keep in them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: confining someone, trapping heat, or bottling up a feeling.
entries.passive: yes — the kids were kept in for recess, the heat is kept in by the storm windows.

entries.meaning: Stay off something, keep something away from it, or avoid a subject.
examples: Keep off the grass.
Doctors told her to keep off the ankle for a week.
A tarp keeps the rain off the woodpile.
This spray keeps off the deer.
The screen is there to keep them off the porch.
Let's keep off politics at dinner.

senses.head: Stay off
body: Prepositional and inseparable; the classic park sign.
examples: Keep off the grass.
Doctors told her to keep off the ankle for a week.

senses.head: Keep something away
body: Separable, with the thing kept away in the middle.
examples: A tarp keeps the rain off the woodpile.
This spray keeps off the deer.
The screen is there to keep them off the porch.

senses.head: Avoid a subject
body: Of conversation topics.
examples: Let's keep off politics at dinner.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress in keep the dog OFF, but off is an unstressed preposition in KEEP off the grass
entries.русский: держаться подальше от; не подпускать; избегать (темы)
entries.separable: yes when there is a thing to keep away — keep the flies off the pie, and with a pronoun it must split: keep them off, never ✗ keep off them. But in keep off the grass, off is a preposition and cannot be separated: ✗ keep the grass off.
entries.transitive: either — an object between the verb and the particle when you keep something away, none there in keep off the grass, where off is a preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: staying off something, warding something off, or steering around a topic.
entries.passive: yes in the separable sense — the flies were kept off the pie. No passive when off is a preposition: ✗ the grass is kept off.
entries.see also: keep away, keep out, hold off

entries.meaning: Carry on doing something, or retain an employee.
examples: He kept on talking through the whole movie.
Keep on walking and don't look back.
The machine kept on running after we cut the power.
They kept two of the interns on after the summer.
She's past retirement age, but they keep her on because nobody else knows the system.
His mother kept on at him about the car.

senses.head: Continue doing
body: Followed by -ing, with a flavor of stubborn repetition.
examples: He kept on talking through the whole movie.
Keep on walking and don't look back.
The machine kept on running after we cut the power.

senses.head: Retain an employee
body: Separable.
examples: They kept two of the interns on after the summer.
She's past retirement age, but they keep her on because nobody else knows the system.

senses.head: keep on at — nag
body: British; an American would say keep after or nag.
examples: His mother kept on at him about the car.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep ON walking, and keep her ON
entries.separable: yes in the employment sense — keep on two of the interns or keep two of the interns on, and with a pronoun it must split: keep her on, never ✗ keep on her. In keep on working, on is fixed to the verb and nothing may come between.
entries.transitive: either — no object before an -ing verb, an object in the employment sense
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: continuing an activity (he kept on talking) or retaining an employee.
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the employment sense: two of the interns were kept on through the fall. No passive of keep on working: ✗ working was kept on.

entries.meaning: Stay outside, or stop something from getting in.
examples: Storm windows keep out the worst of the cold.
The fence keeps the deer out.
It's a good screen — it keeps them out all summer.
Keep out — construction area.
Keep out of it; this is between them.

senses.head: Stop from entering
body: Separable, and the split order is at least as common.
examples: Storm windows keep out the worst of the cold.
The fence keeps the deer out.
It's a good screen — it keeps them out all summer.

senses.head: Stay outside, stay uninvolved
body: No object; what you stay out of follows of.
examples: Keep out — construction area.
Keep out of it; this is between them.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep it OUT
entries.separable: yes — keep out the cold or keep the cold out, and with a pronoun it must split: keep it out, never ✗ keep out it. On a sign it takes no object at all: KEEP OUT.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you exclude something, none in the warning keep out
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, causative in sense 1 (something prevents entry) and a plain act of staying outside in sense 2. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the exclusion sense — the deer are kept out by the fence, most of the cold is kept out by storm windows. No passive of the object-less warning: ✗ it was kept out for the sign KEEP OUT.
entries.see also: keep in, keep away, let in

entries.meaning: Stick to a plan, a route, or a rule; or keep something private.
examples: Please keep to the agenda.
Keep to the right on the stairs.
We kept to the budget within a few hundred dollars.
Keep this to yourself until it's announced.
He kept his diagnosis to himself.
The new neighbor keeps to himself.

senses.head: Stick to, not depart from
body: Of a schedule, a budget, a subject, a lane.
examples: Please keep to the agenda.
Keep to the right on the stairs.
We kept to the budget within a few hundred dollars.

senses.head: keep something to yourself — not tell
body: The thing sits in the middle and the reflexive pronoun follows.
examples: Keep this to yourself until it's announced.
He kept his diagnosis to himself.

senses.head: keep to yourself — stay solitary
body: About a person's habits rather than a secret.
examples: The new neighbor keeps to himself.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — KEEP to the schedule; to stays weak
entries.separable: no — the object follows to: keep to the schedule, ✗ keep the schedule to; with a pronoun, keep to it, ✗ keep it to. The one exception is the fixed keep something to yourself, where the thing goes in the middle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (sticking to a plan, withholding a fact); sense 3, the neighbor keeps to himself, describes a settled habit and is close to stative, though the progressive is still fine (he's been keeping to himself lately).
entries.passive: restricted — natural when a middle object can be promoted: costs were kept to a minimum, the diagnosis was kept to a handful of people. The prepositional passive of sense 1 is stiff in American English: ?the agenda was not kept to, where a speaker would say nobody stuck to the agenda.

entries.meaning: Maintain something, continue it, avoid falling behind, or prevent someone from sleeping.
examples: They can't afford to keep up the house anymore.
Keep the pressure up on the wound.
You're doing great — keep it up.
I had to jog to keep up.
Slow down, I can't keep up.
The neighbors' party kept us up until two.
Sorry to keep you up — this won't take long.

senses.head: Maintain, not let decline
body: Separable. Of a house, a payment schedule, a standard, a friendship.
examples: They can't afford to keep up the house anymore.
Keep the pressure up on the wound.
You're doing great — keep it up.

senses.head: Not fall behind
body: No object; who or what you match follows with.
examples: I had to jog to keep up.
Slow down, I can't keep up.

senses.head: Prevent from sleeping
body: The person sits between the verb and the particle.
examples: The neighbors' party kept us up until two.
Sorry to keep you up — this won't take long.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — keep it UP, never KEEP it up
entries.русский: поддерживать; продолжать; не отставать; не давать спать
entries.separable: yes — keep up the good work or keep the pressure up, and with a pronoun it must split: keep it up, never ✗ keep up it. In the "not fall behind" sense there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you maintain something, none when you avoid falling behind
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense — maintaining a house, matching a pace, keeping someone awake. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the property has been beautifully kept up, we were kept up until two by the neighbors. No passive of the object-less sense 2: ✗ it was kept up with for I couldn't keep up.
entries.see also: keep up with, keep on, hold up

entries.meaning: Move or progress at the same rate as something, stay informed about it, or stay in touch.
examples: Wages haven't kept up with rent.
He can't keep up with the other kids on the hill.
Production is barely keeping up with orders.
I don't keep up with the news the way I used to.
She keeps up with every change in the tax code.
We've kept up with each other since college.
The whole cul-de-sac is keeping up with the Joneses.

senses.head: Match the pace of
body: Of a walker, a class, inflation, demand.
examples: Wages haven't kept up with rent.
He can't keep up with the other kids on the hill.
Production is barely keeping up with orders.

senses.head: Stay informed about
body: Of news, a field, a show.
examples: I don't keep up with the news the way I used to.
She keeps up with every change in the tax code.

senses.head: Stay in touch with
body: Of friends and family.
examples: We've kept up with each other since college.

senses.head: keep up with the Joneses — match the neighbors' spending
body: A fixed American idiom, mildly mocking.
examples: The whole cul-de-sac is keeping up with the Joneses.

entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle carries the stress — keep UP with them
entries.русский: успевать за, поспевать; следить за (новостями); поддерживать связь
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Keep up with the class, ✗ keep the class up with; with a pronoun, keep up with them, ✗ keep them up with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the pace sense (wages haven't kept up with rent) and the informed sense (I don't keep up with the news) both take the progressive freely — she's keeping up with the tax code.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is grammatical but stiff and rare: ?rent has not been kept up with, ?the news is not kept up with the way it used to be. American speakers recast in the active, and the fixed idiom has none: ✗ the Joneses were kept up with.

entries.meaning: Be aware that someone or something exists, without necessarily knowing them. Know alone would claim acquaintance; know of only claims awareness.
examples: I know of a good mechanic on Ferry Street.
Do you know of any reason the closing would be delayed?
Not that I know of.
She knew of him by reputation but had never met him.
I know of two other families with the same problem.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — not that I KNOW of; of reduces to /əv/
entries.separable: no — the object always follows of. I know of a good mechanic, ✗ I know a good mechanic of; with a pronoun, I know of it, ✗ I know it of.
entries.verb type: stative — a state of awareness, not an act. It rejects the progressive: ✗ I am knowing of a good mechanic, and it has no habitual or dynamic use.
entries.passive: no — a stative prepositional verb, so the object cannot be promoted: ✗ a good mechanic is known of by me, ✗ no reason is known of. The idiomatic not that I know of is frozen in the active. (The passive he is well known belongs to plain know, not to know of.)

entries.meaning: Put something down for later, or abandon a feeling or an argument.
examples: He laid the letter aside and rubbed his eyes.
She laid aside her knitting when the phone rang.
The novel bored her and she laid it aside after forty pages.
They lay aside a little every month for the girls' tuition.
We had a hundred dollars laid aside for emergencies.
The two families finally laid aside their quarrel.
Lay aside your objections for one minute and hear the plan.

senses.head: Put down for the moment
body: Separable and literal, of an object in your hands.
examples: He laid the letter aside and rubbed his eyes.
She laid aside her knitting when the phone rang.
The novel bored her and she laid it aside after forty pages.

senses.head: Save for the future
body: Of money, food, supplies.
examples: They lay aside a little every month for the girls' tuition.
We had a hundred dollars laid aside for emergencies.

senses.head: Give up, set down a feeling
body: Of grudges, differences, doubts, formality.
examples: The two families finally laid aside their quarrel.
Lay aside your objections for one minute and hear the plan.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay it aSIDE
entries.separable: yes — lay aside the book or lay the book aside, and with a pronoun it must split: lay it aside, never ✗ lay aside it.
entries.register: formal — the everyday equivalents are put aside and set aside
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses, from the physical putting-down to the figurative giving-up of a grudge. The participle laid aside also works as a plain adjective: the money laid aside for tuition.
entries.passive: yes, and it is common in the saving and abandoning senses — a hundred dollars had been laid aside for emergencies, the quarrel was finally laid aside. Never ✗ was lain aside: the verb is lay, whose participle is laid.

entries.meaning: Set something aside for later; in a store, reserve goods against a deposit until they are paid off.
examples: She laid away a winter coat in September and paid it off by December.
The store will lay the bike away for twenty dollars down.
They laid away enough firewood for two winters.
It's on hold in the back — they laid it away for you.
Before credit cards, families laid away Christmas gifts all fall.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay it aWAY
entries.separable: yes — lay away a coat or lay a coat away, and with a pronoun it must split: lay it away, never ✗ lay away it.
entries.register: everyday — the store sense is American; the noun layaway comes from it
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a physical setting-aside or a store transaction. No stative or linking use; the noun layaway is derived from it.
entries.passive: yes — the coat was laid away in September and paid off by December, enough firewood was laid away for two winters. In a store an American more often says it's on layaway.
entries.see also: lay aside, lay in, lay up

entries.meaning: Put something down, or set out a rule as something not open to argument. Note that lay down takes an object and lie down does not: you lay the baby down, but you lie down yourself.
examples: He laid his tools down and looked up.
Lay down the tarp before you open the paint.
That frame is cracked, so lay it down gently.
The contract lays down exactly who pays for repairs.
Her father laid down the law about weeknights.
They laid strict conditions down before agreeing.
The garrison laid down its arms at dawn.
They laid down the vocals in one afternoon.

senses.head: Put down
body: Separable and literal.
examples: He laid his tools down and looked up.
Lay down the tarp before you open the paint.
That frame is cracked, so lay it down gently.

senses.head: Establish a rule
body: Fixed in lay down the law, lay down conditions, lay down guidelines.
examples: The contract lays down exactly who pays for repairs.
Her father laid down the law about weeknights.
They laid strict conditions down before agreeing.

senses.head: Surrender weapons
body: Fixed in lay down your arms / your weapons.
examples: The garrison laid down its arms at dawn.

senses.head: Record a track
body: Informal, from the studio.
examples: They laid down the vocals in one afternoon.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay it DOWN
entries.separable: yes — lay down the law or lay the law down, and with a pronoun it must split: lay it down, never ✗ lay down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: putting a thing down, issuing a rule, surrendering arms, recording a track.
entries.passive: yes, and the rule sense lives mostly in the passive — the terms are laid down in section 4, the garrison's arms were laid down at dawn, the vocals were laid down in one afternoon. Never ✗ was lain down.
entries.see also: lie around, lay out, lay off

entries.meaning: Buy and store a supply of something before you need it.
examples: They laid in enough firewood for the whole winter.
The kitchen lays in two hundred pounds of flour every fall.
We'd laid a case of water in before the hurricane.
Lay in some candles — the power goes out here constantly.
The salt was cheap in August, so we laid it in then.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay IN supplies
entries.separable: yes — lay in a supply of salt or lay a supply of salt in, though the unsplit order is the usual one; with a pronoun it must split: lay it in, never ✗ lay in it.
entries.register: formal — a little old-fashioned; most Americans say stock up on
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a deliberate act of stocking up. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — enough firewood had been laid in for the whole winter, the salt was laid in back in August, though the active is far commoner and most Americans say stocked up on.

entries.meaning: Attack someone, usually with words but sometimes with fists.
examples: The coach laid into the team at halftime.
She laid into him for missing the deadline.
Reviewers laid into the movie before it even opened wide.
