Two of them laid into each other in the parking lot.
Don't lay into the kid; he was following instructions.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — he LAID into me; into is a preposition and keeps its object behind it
entries.separable: no — the object always follows into. He laid into the referee, ✗ he laid the referee into; with a pronoun, she laid into him, ✗ she laid him into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an attack in words or fists. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive is grammatical but rare and stiff in American English: ?the referee was laid into by the coach. Speakers recast in the active or switch verbs — he got chewed out, she tore into him.
entries.see also: hit back, hit out, hold forth

entries.meaning: Dismiss workers because there is no work, or stop doing something.
examples: The plant laid off three hundred people in March.
They laid the whole night shift off without warning.
He'd been there eleven years when they laid him off.
Lay off the sugar for a week and see how you feel.
Lay off him — he just got here.

senses.head: Dismiss for economic reasons
body: Separable. It is not the same as firing: a layoff blames the business, not the worker. The noun is layoff.
examples: The plant laid off three hundred people in March.
They laid the whole night shift off without warning.
He'd been there eleven years when they laid him off.

senses.head: Stop, ease up on
body: Informal and inseparable, since off here is a preposition. Often an imperative.
examples: Lay off the sugar for a week and see how you feel.
Lay off him — he just got here.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress in the firing sense — lay them OFF; but in LAY off the doughnuts, off is an unstressed preposition
entries.separable: yes in the employment sense — lay off two hundred workers or lay two hundred workers off, and with a pronoun it must split: lay them off, never ✗ lay off them. In the "stop" sense off is a preposition and cannot be split: lay off him means leave him alone, while lay him off means fire him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; sense 2 is nearly always an imperative (lay off the sugar), which is dynamic by definition. The noun layoff comes from sense 1.
entries.passive: yes in the employment sense, where the passive is the usual way to say it — three hundred people were laid off in March, he was laid off after eleven years. The "stop" sense has no passive: ✗ the sugar was laid off, ✗ he was laid off meaning leave him alone (that reading is only the firing one).
entries.see also: let off, let up, lay up

entries.meaning: Apply something to a surface, pile on praise or blame, or (in British English) provide something for guests.
examples: Lay on a second coat once this one dries.
He laid the mortar on too thick and it sagged.
He really laid it on thick about how much he missed us.
She's not wrong, but she lays it on a little.
The company laid on a bus to the airport.
All right, lay it on me — how much is the repair?

senses.head: Apply to a surface
body: Separable, of paint, plaster, frosting.
examples: Lay on a second coat once this one dries.
He laid the mortar on too thick and it sagged.

senses.head: lay it on thick — exaggerate
body: Fixed and informal, about flattery or a sob story.
examples: He really laid it on thick about how much he missed us.
She's not wrong, but she lays it on a little.

senses.head: Provide, put on for people
body: British. An American would say put on or provide.
examples: The company laid on a bus to the airport.

senses.head: lay it on me — tell me
body: Informal and American, inviting bad news.
examples: All right, lay it on me — how much is the repair?

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay it ON thick
entries.separable: yes — lay on another coat or lay another coat on, and with a pronoun it must split: lay it on, never ✗ lay on it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: applying a coat, piling on flattery, providing a bus.
entries.passive: yes in the applying and providing senses — a second coat was laid on once the first dried, a bus was laid on to the airport (British). The fixed idioms resist it: ✗ I was laid it on for lay it on me, and the flattery was laid on thick only works once you replace it with a real noun.

entries.meaning: Spread something out, explain it clearly, spend money on it, or knock someone unconscious.
examples: She laid out her clothes the night before.
He laid the blueprints out on the hood of the truck.
The town was laid out on a grid in 1847.
The memo lays out three options.
Lay it out for me in plain English.
We laid out two thousand dollars on that transmission.
One punch laid him out.

senses.head: Spread out, arrange
body: Separable. Of clothes, tools, a garden, a page.
examples: She laid out her clothes the night before.
He laid the blueprints out on the hood of the truck.
The town was laid out on a grid in 1847.

senses.head: Explain step by step
body: Of a plan, a case, an argument.
examples: The memo lays out three options.
Lay it out for me in plain English.

senses.head: Spend money
body: Informal, and usually about a painful amount.
examples: We laid out two thousand dollars on that transmission.

senses.head: Knock unconscious
body: Informal.
examples: One punch laid him out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay it OUT
entries.separable: yes — lay out the plan or lay the plan out, and with a pronoun it must split: lay it out, never ✗ lay out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses — arranging, explaining, spending, knocking out. The participle doubles as an adjective in a well laid-out kitchen.
entries.passive: yes throughout, and it is the natural form for senses 1 and 2 — the town was laid out on a grid in 1847, three options are laid out in the memo, he was laid out by one punch.
entries.see also: lay on, lay down, hold forth

entries.meaning: Break a journey and wait somewhere between flights or legs of a trip.
examples: We lay over in Denver for four hours.
The crew laid over in Anchorage and flew out the next morning.
If you lay over in Chicago, get the pizza in Terminal 1.
I'd rather lay over than take the red-eye.
They laid over two nights in Reykjavik and called it a vacation.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lay Over in Denver
entries.separable: n/a — it takes no object; the city follows in.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.register: everyday — American; British English says stop over. The noun layover comes from it
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of breaking a journey. Intransitive only; no stative or linking use. The noun layover comes from it.
entries.passive: no — the verb takes no object, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ Denver was laid over in, ✗ four hours were laid over. Only the noun survives in we had a four-hour layover.

entries.meaning: Put someone out of action with illness or injury, or put something into storage.
examples: He was laid up for a month with a slipped disk.
A bad ankle laid her up through the playoffs.
The flu laid half the office up.
They laid up enough jam to last two winters.
The ferry is laid up for repairs until April.

senses.head: Confine with illness or injury
body: Usually passive. Very often laid up with a named ailment.
examples: He was laid up for a month with a slipped disk.
A bad ankle laid her up through the playoffs.
The flu laid half the office up.

senses.head: Store for the future
body: Of supplies, preserves, provisions.
examples: They laid up enough jam to last two winters.

senses.head: Take out of service
body: Of boats, planes, and rolling stock.
examples: The ferry is laid up for repairs until April.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — laid him UP for a week
entries.русский: выводить из строя (о болезни); откладывать про запас; ставить на прикол
entries.separable: yes — lay up the boat or lay the boat up, and with a pronoun it must split: it laid him up, never ✗ it laid up him. The illness sense is almost always passive: he was laid up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: disabling someone, storing supplies, taking a vessel out of service.
entries.passive: yes, and the illness sense is normally passive — he was laid up for a month with a slipped disk, the ferry is laid up for repairs until April. The active a bad ankle laid her up is the other common shape.
entries.see also: lay in, lay off, hold up

entries.meaning: Go first, begin something, or take someone away.
examples: She led off with a joke about the parking.
The paper led off with the flood story.
The chairman led off the meeting with the budget.
You take the first question and lead it off.
He led off the ninth with a double.
Two deputies led him off in handcuffs.

senses.head: Begin, go first
body: No object; what you begin with follows with.
examples: She led off with a joke about the parking.
The paper led off with the flood story.

senses.head: Begin something specific
body: Separable.
examples: The chairman led off the meeting with the budget.
You take the first question and lead it off.

senses.head: Bat first in an inning
body: American baseball, where the leadoff hitter is the first batter.
examples: He led off the ninth with a double.

senses.head: Take someone away
body: Separable, and usually of police.
examples: Two deputies led him off in handcuffs.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lead OFF, and lead it OFF
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — lead off the meeting or lead the meeting off, and with a pronoun it must split: lead it off, never ✗ lead off it. It is just as often used with no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you begin something specific, none when you simply go first
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses — beginning, batting first, escorting someone away. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes where there is an object — the meeting was led off with the budget, he was led off in handcuffs. No passive of the object-less sense 1: ✗ it was led off with a joke when the point is that she began with one.

entries.meaning: Keep someone hoping for something you have no intention of giving, especially in a romance.
examples: She wasn't interested; she was just leading him on.
The seller led us on for three weeks and then took another offer.
Don't lead the kid on if you're not going to hire him.
He felt led on by the whole interview process.
Leading people on is worse than saying no.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lead him ON
entries.separable: yes, and the split order is the usual one — lead the buyer on, and with a pronoun it must split: lead him on, never ✗ lead on him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a sustained act of misleading someone. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, and it is very common — he felt led on by the whole interview process, the buyers were led on for three weeks and then dropped.

entries.meaning: Have something as a result. The chain may be long — this is about consequence, not about walking somewhere.
examples: The audit led to three resignations.
One thing led to another and they were married by June.
Cutting the night bus led to people quitting jobs they couldn't reach.
Nobody knows what led to the fire.
That conversation led to the biggest change of my career.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — that LED to the merger; to stays weak
entries.separable: no — the result always follows to. One thing led to another, ✗ one thing led another to; with a pronoun, what led to it?, ✗ what led it to?.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in form, but the meaning is a relation of consequence rather than anything an agent does; the subject is normally an event, not a person. The progressive is fine: this is leading to a lawsuit.
entries.passive: no — the object after to is a result, not a patient, so it cannot be promoted: ✗ three resignations were led to by the audit, ✗ the fire was led to by faulty wiring. Use resulted from or was caused by instead.

entries.meaning: Come before something and prepare the way for it; or approach a subject gradually.
examples: In the weeks leading up to the election, nobody slept.
Everything that led up to the crash is in the report.
The training leads up to a certification exam.
I could tell he was leading up to asking for money.
She led up to the bad news so carefully that I guessed it first.

senses.head: Precede and prepare for
body: Very often in the participle: the days leading up to.
examples: In the weeks leading up to the election, nobody slept.
Everything that led up to the crash is in the report.
The training leads up to a certification exam.

senses.head: Approach a topic gradually
body: Of a person circling around what they actually want to say.
examples: I could tell he was leading up to asking for money.
She led up to the bad news so carefully that I guessed it first.

entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle carries the stress — lead UP to it
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. The weeks leading up to the vote, ✗ the weeks leading the vote up to; with a pronoun, leading up to it, ✗ leading it up to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but relational like lead to: the subject is usually a stretch of time or a series of events, and the commonest form is the participle — the weeks leading up to the vote.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the election was led up to by weeks of ads, ✗ the request was led up to. There is no idiomatic passive in either sense; the participial active does all the work.

entries.meaning: Rest your weight on something, rely on someone, or pressure someone.
examples: She leaned on her sister the whole year after the divorce.
Small towns lean on volunteers for everything.
The contractor leaned on the inspector to sign off.
Somebody leaned on him and he changed his story.
Don't lean on that railing; it's loose.

senses.head: Rely on for support
body: Emotional or practical, and the most common figurative use.
examples: She leaned on her sister the whole year after the divorce.
Small towns lean on volunteers for everything.

senses.head: Pressure, intimidate
body: Informal, with a faint whiff of the mob movie.
examples: The contractor leaned on the inspector to sign off.
Somebody leaned on him and he changed his story.

senses.head: Rest your weight on
body: The literal sense, from which the others grow.
examples: Don't lean on that railing; it's loose.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — she LEANS on her sister; on is a preposition and keeps its object behind it
entries.русский: опираться на, рассчитывать на; давить на
entries.separable: no — the object always follows on. He leaned on his brother, ✗ he leaned his brother on; with a pronoun, lean on him, ✗ lean him on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses, including the figurative reliance (small towns lean on volunteers), which takes the progressive freely: she's been leaning on her sister all year.
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the pressure sense, where it is common: the inspector was leaned on to sign off, he'd clearly been leaned on. Stiff in the reliance sense: ?her sister was leaned on the whole year.

entries.meaning: Be inclined to prefer or believe something, without having decided.
examples: I'm leaning toward the second candidate.
The committee leans toward rebuilding rather than repairing.
She leaned toward staying home, but he had the tickets.
Most of the panel leaned toward acquittal by the third day.
We hadn't decided, but we were leaning toward it.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — I LEAN toward the second one
entries.separable: no — the object always follows toward. I lean toward the cheaper plan, ✗ I lean the cheaper plan toward; with a pronoun, I lean toward it, ✗ I lean it toward.
entries.register: everyday — Americans write toward, the British towards
entries.verb type: stative — an inclination of mind rather than an act; nothing is done. Unusually for a stative it takes the progressive comfortably, and I'm leaning toward the second candidate is the commonest form of all.
entries.passive: no — the object is a preference, not a patient: ✗ the cheaper plan is leaned toward by the committee, ✗ acquittal was leaned toward. Recast as the committee favors or the committee is inclined toward.

entries.meaning: Accept an opportunity instantly and eagerly. American English prefers the past leaped; leapt is also correct.
examples: She leaped at the chance to transfer.
He leaped at the first offer and regretted it by Friday.
Any of us would have leaped at that salary.
They leapt at the invitation.
It was a bad contract, but he was broke, so he leaped at it.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — she LEAPED at the chance; at reduces to /ət/
entries.separable: no — the object always follows at. He leaped at the offer, ✗ he leaped the offer at; with a pronoun, she leaped at it, ✗ she leaped it at.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and punctual: it names the instant of accepting, not a stretch of consideration.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but not idiomatic in American English: ?the offer was leaped at, ?that salary would have been leapt at by any of us. The active is what people say.

entries.meaning: Be so obvious that it seems to jump at you; also, jump out from hiding.
examples: The typo leaps out at you in the headline.
One line in the contract leaped out at me.
Nothing in the data leaps out as unusual.
A deer leaped out in front of the car.
He leaped out of the truck before it stopped rolling.

senses.head: Be immediately obvious
body: Of a mistake, a name, a number on a page. Almost always with at.
examples: The typo leaps out at you in the headline.
One line in the contract leaped out at me.
Nothing in the data leaps out as unusual.

senses.head: Jump out suddenly
body: The literal sense.
examples: A deer leaped out in front of the car.
He leaped out of the truck before it stopped rolling.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — it leaped OUT at me
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object; the person it strikes follows at, as in leaped out at me.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes a direct object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: the literal jump, and the perceptual sense in which a mistake seems to jump at the reader.
entries.passive: no — there is no direct object, only the at-phrase, and the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ I was leaped out at by a deer, ✗ the reader is leaped out at.

entries.meaning: Come to know that something has happened, usually through an official or written channel.
examples: The family learned of his death from a reporter.
We learned of the merger only when the filing became public.
She learned of the award in a letter.
Investors learned of the recall three weeks after the company did.
If you learn of any change of address, notify the court.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — we LEARNED of it later; of reduces to /əv/
entries.separable: no — the object always follows of. We learned of the merger, ✗ we learned the merger of; with a pronoun, we learned of it, ✗ we learned it of.
entries.register: formal — in speech Americans say hear about or find out about
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and inchoative: it names the moment of coming to know, which is why it pairs with a point in time (we learned of it on Tuesday). Contrast the stative know of, which names the state that follows.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ his death was learned of by the family, ✗ the recall was learned of three weeks later. Writers recast in the active or use it emerged that….
entries.see also: hear of, hear about, know of

entries.meaning: Set a question aside for the moment so you can deal with the rest.
examples: Leaving aside the cost, is the design even legal?
Let's leave the parking question aside until we have the traffic study.
He left aside the personal history and stuck to the numbers.
Leave it aside for a second — what does the contract say?
The report leaves aside everything that happened before 2019.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — leave it aSIDE
entries.separable: yes — leave aside the cost or leave the cost aside, and with a pronoun it must split: leave it aside, never ✗ leave aside it.
entries.register: formal — commonest in the participle, leaving aside the question of...
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of setting a question outside the discussion. Commonest as a participial adjunct: leaving aside the cost….
entries.passive: yes — the personal history was left aside, everything before 2019 is left aside in the report. The active participle is still the form you meet most.

entries.meaning: Go without something or someone, outpace them, or leave something after you.
examples: I left my phone behind at the restaurant.
Leave behind anything you can't carry uphill.
The kit was on the counter and she left it behind.
He left the rest of the field behind on the last lap.
The town got left behind when the mill closed.
She left behind a husband and two daughters.
The storm left behind four feet of water.

senses.head: Not take with you, forget
body: Separable, and the split order is the everyday one.
examples: I left my phone behind at the restaurant.
Leave behind anything you can't carry uphill.
The kit was on the counter and she left it behind.

senses.head: Outdistance, surpass
body: Of runners, rivals, and whole towns.
examples: He left the rest of the field behind on the last lap.
The town got left behind when the mill closed.

senses.head: Leave after you
body: Of survivors, a mess, a legacy.
examples: She left behind a husband and two daughters.
The storm left behind four feet of water.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — leave it behIND
entries.русский: оставлять, забывать; обгонять; оставлять после себя
entries.separable: yes — leave behind the heavy gear or leave the heavy gear behind, and with a pronoun it must split: leave it behind, never ✗ leave behind it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — forgetting, outdistancing, leaving something after you. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, and it is common — the town got left behind when the mill closed, four feet of water was left behind by the storm, my phone was left behind at the restaurant.

entries.meaning: Stop at a point, or omit something.
examples: Let's pick up where we left off.
I forget where I left off in the book.
They left my name off the invitation.
Leave off the middle initial; the form won't take it.
It's a small thing, but you left it off the invoice.
Leave off teasing your sister.

senses.head: Stop at a point
body: No object, and nearly always in where we left off.
examples: Let's pick up where we left off.
I forget where I left off in the book.

senses.head: Omit from a list
body: Separable.
examples: They left my name off the invitation.
Leave off the middle initial; the form won't take it.
It's a small thing, but you left it off the invoice.

senses.head: Stop doing
body: A little old-fashioned in American English, where quit or stop is usual.
examples: Leave off teasing your sister.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — leave it OFF, and pick up where we left OFF
entries.separable: yes when it has an object — leave off the last name or leave the last name off, and with a pronoun it must split: leave it off, never ✗ leave off it. In where we left off there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you omit something, none when you stop
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, stopping and omitting. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes in the omission sense — my name was left off the invitation, the middle initial can be left off. No passive of the object-less stopping sense: ✗ where was left off for where we left off.

entries.meaning: Fail or decline to include something or someone.
examples: You left out the best part of the story.
He left two payments out of the ledger.
It's a long recipe — leave it out if you don't have any.
Nobody meant to leave her out.
The youngest always feels left out at these things.

senses.head: Omit
body: Separable, and the commonest sense by far.
examples: You left out the best part of the story.
He left two payments out of the ledger.
It's a long recipe — leave it out if you don't have any.

senses.head: Exclude a person
body: Very often passive, as feel left out.
examples: Nobody meant to leave her out.
The youngest always feels left out at these things.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — leave it OUT
entries.separable: yes — leave out the details or leave the details out, and with a pronoun it must split: leave it out, never ✗ leave out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, omitting and excluding. The participle is also a plain adjective in the left-out kid.
entries.passive: yes, and the exclusion sense usually appears that way — the youngest always feels left out, the best part of the story was left out, two payments were left out of the ledger.
entries.see also: leave off, leave behind, let in on

entries.meaning: Have something remain unused or uneaten after everything else is gone.
examples: There were three slices left over.
Whatever money is left over goes back to the fund.
We had a whole tray of ziti left over.
The committee left the vote over until October.
They left it over to the next session.

senses.head: be left over — remain
body: The usual form. The noun leftovers is what is in the fridge on Friday.
examples: There were three slices left over.
Whatever money is left over goes back to the fund.
We had a whole tray of ziti left over.

senses.head: Postpone to a later meeting
body: British; Americans say hold over.
examples: The committee left the vote over until October.
They left it over to the next session.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — two slices were left Over
entries.separable: yes — leave over the vote or leave the vote over, and with a pronoun it must split: they left it over, never ✗ they left over it. In the "remain" sense you will meet it far more often in the passive, be left over, and as the adjective and noun leftover.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 is normally frozen in the passive participle left over, which behaves as an adjective (the leftover ziti) and gives the noun leftovers.
entries.passive: yes, and for sense 1 the passive is essentially the only form — there were three slices left over, whatever money is left over goes back to the fund. Sense 2 passivizes too: the vote was left over until October (British).

entries.meaning: Be well suited to a particular use or treatment. The subject is the thing being used, not the person using it.
examples: The novel lends itself to film better than most.
That corner room lends itself to a nursery.
Cast iron lends itself to high heat.
The data don't lend themselves to a simple chart.
A short poem lends itself to memorization in a way a long one does not.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the reflexive pronoun in the middle — lends itSELF to it
entries.separable: no — nothing may come between the three parts, and the reflexive pronoun can never move behind to: the book lends itself to adaptation, ✗ the book lends to itself adaptation. The pronoun must also agree with the subject: these rooms lend themselves to it, ✗ these rooms lend itself to it.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after to
entries.verb type: stative — it reports a property of the subject, that something is suited to a use; nobody does anything. It resists the progressive: ✗ that room is lending itself to a nursery. Note the reflexive must agree — the data lend themselves to, ✗ lend itself to.
entries.passive: no — the object of the verb is the reflexive pronoun, and a reflexive can never become a passive subject: ✗ itself is lent to adaptation by the novel, ✗ film is lent itself to. Stative meaning blocks it a second time; recast as the novel is well suited to film.

entries.meaning: Let someone take something away for a while, expecting it back.
examples: The library lends out hotspots as well as books.
He lent his good drill out and never saw it again.
Don't lend that out — it's the only copy.
They lend out folding chairs to anyone in the neighborhood.
I'd lend it out to you, but my brother has it.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lend it OUT
entries.separable: yes — lend out the tools or lend the tools out, and with a pronoun it must split: lend it out, never ✗ lend out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a transfer with an expectation of return. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — hotspots are lent out for three weeks at a time, the drill was lent out and never came back. Both lent and (rarely, nonstandard) loaned out are heard in America; lent is the safe participle.

entries.meaning: Disappoint someone who was counting on you; also, lower something. The noun letdown is the disappointment.
examples: I promised I'd be there, and I let them down.
Don't let your grandmother down twice in one week.
The sequel let everyone down.
They let down a rope from the window.
Let the tailgate down so we can slide it in.
He never lets his hair down in front of the staff.

senses.head: Disappoint
body: The main sense. The object is a person, and the split order is the usual one — with a pronoun it is the only one.
examples: I promised I'd be there, and I let them down.
Don't let your grandmother down twice in one week.
The sequel let everyone down.

senses.head: Lower
body: Literal, of a rope, a bucket, a window, a hem.
examples: They let down a rope from the window.
Let the tailgate down so we can slide it in.

senses.head: let your hair down — relax
body: A fixed idiom, informal.
examples: He never lets his hair down in front of the staff.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — let me DOWN, never LET me down
entries.separable: yes — let down the team or let the team down, and with a pronoun it must split: let me down, never ✗ let down me. With a person as object the split order is far the commoner one; with a thing, both orders are equally at home: let down the rope or let the rope down.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, disappointing and lowering. The noun letdown comes from sense 1.
entries.passive: yes — everyone was let down by the sequel, a rope was let down from the window. The idiom does not passivize: ✗ his hair was let down in the sense of relaxing.

entries.meaning: Allow someone or something to come inside.
examples: Let the dog in — it's pouring.
Nobody was at the desk, so a nurse let us in.
They wouldn't let in anyone without a badge.
These old windows let in a lot of cold.
The right boot lets water in.
He had no idea what he was letting himself in for.

senses.head: Admit a person or animal
body: Separable.
examples: Let the dog in — it's pouring.
Nobody was at the desk, so a nurse let us in.
They wouldn't let in anyone without a badge.

senses.head: Admit light, water, air
body: Of windows, roofs, and boots.
examples: These old windows let in a lot of cold.
The right boot lets water in.

senses.head: let yourself in for — bring trouble on yourself
body: Fixed and always about something unpleasant.
examples: He had no idea what he was letting himself in for.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — let him IN
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun it must split: let me in, never ✗ let in me. With a noun both orders work: let in the dog or let the dog in.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of admitting a person or of a material admitting cold, water, or light. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — we were let in by a nurse, nobody was let in without a badge. The fixed let yourself in for has no passive: ✗ he was let in for a lot of trouble.
entries.see also: let in on, keep out, let out

entries.meaning: Tell someone a secret that other people already share.
examples: Are you going to let me in on the joke?
They let him in on the surprise a week early.
Only three people were let in on the plan.
She let her sister in on the pregnancy before anyone else.
If you're going to keep the account, let the new hire in on the history.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle takes the stress — let me IN on it
entries.separable: yes, and it must split — the person sits between let and in and the secret follows on: let the new hire in on the plan, and with a pronoun let me in on the plan, ✗ let in me on the plan, ✗ let in on me the plan.
entries.transitive: yes — a person before in and a thing after on
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act of disclosure to a chosen person.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual way to report it from the secret's side — only three people were let in on the plan, I was never let in on the joke.
entries.see also: let on, let in, hold out on

entries.meaning: Excuse someone from punishment or duty, release something, or drop a passenger.
examples: The judge let him off with a fine.
The officer let us off with a warning.
They let off the two youngest and charged the rest.
Her boss let her off early on Fridays.
Somebody let off fireworks at two in the morning.
He goes to the batting cage to let off steam.
Let me off at the corner.

senses.head: Excuse from punishment
body: Separable. Often let off with a warning, or let off easy.
examples: The judge let him off with a fine.
The officer let us off with a warning.
They let off the two youngest and charged the rest.

senses.head: Excuse from a duty
body: Of chores, work, obligations.
examples: Her boss let her off early on Fridays.

senses.head: Release, emit
body: Of steam, fireworks, a smell. Let off steam means release frustration.
examples: Somebody let off fireworks at two in the morning.
He goes to the batting cage to let off steam.

senses.head: Drop a passenger
body: American; British English says let out or drop off.
examples: Let me off at the corner.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — let him OFF
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun it must split: let him off, never ✗ let off him. With a noun both orders work: let off the passengers or let the passengers off.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses — excusing, releasing, emitting, dropping a passenger.
entries.passive: yes, and sense 1 is most often passive — he was let off with a warning, the two youngest were let off, fireworks were let off at two in the morning, we were let off at the corner.
entries.see also: lay off, let out, let up

entries.meaning: Show or admit that you know something, usually in the negative.
examples: Don't let on that I told you.
She knew the whole time and never let on.
He didn't let on how sick he was.
If they ask, don't let on — act surprised.
The kids figured it out but never let on to their parents.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — don't let ON
entries.separable: no — a noun object never comes between the verb and the particle; what follows is a that-clause, not an object: he never let on that he knew, ✗ he never let the secret on.
entries.transitive: either — usually no object at all, sometimes a that-clause
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an act (or, usually, the refusal of an act) of disclosure. Almost always negated: she never let on.
entries.passive: no — there is no object to promote; what follows is a that-clause or nothing at all: ✗ that he knew was let on, ✗ how sick he was was let on. Use it was never revealed that… instead.
entries.see also: let in on, hold out on

entries.meaning: Release something, make a garment wider, produce a sound, or come to an end.
examples: Let the dog out before you leave.
They let out the prisoners who had served their time.
The cat's crying at the door — let her out.
The tailor let out the waist an inch.
She let out a scream that woke the block.
He let out a long breath and sat down.
School lets out at three-fifteen.

senses.head: Release, allow out
body: Separable.
examples: Let the dog out before you leave.
They let out the prisoners who had served their time.
The cat's crying at the door — let her out.

senses.head: Make a garment wider
body: The opposite of take in.
examples: The tailor let out the waist an inch.

senses.head: Produce a sound
body: Of a scream, a sigh, a laugh.
examples: She let out a scream that woke the block.
He let out a long breath and sat down.

senses.head: End, finish for the day
body: No object. American, of school, class, church, and movies.
examples: School lets out at three-fifteen.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — let it OUT
entries.separable: yes, and with a pronoun it must split: let it out, never ✗ let out it. With a noun both orders work: let out the dog or let the dog out. In school lets out at three there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — an object in most senses, none when a class or a movie ends
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses — releasing, widening a garment, producing a sound, ending for the day.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the prisoners were let out, the waist was let out an inch, a scream was let out (stiff; the active is better). No passive of sense 4: ✗ three-fifteen is let out at for school lets out at three-fifteen.
entries.see also: let in, let off, lend out

entries.meaning: Become less intense, or ease the pressure on someone.
examples: The rain let up just after noon.
The headaches haven't let up all week.
Business won't let up until January.
Let up on him — he's been here two days.
The defense never let up on the quarterback.

senses.head: Become less intense
body: Of rain, wind, pain, pressure, work.
examples: The rain let up just after noon.
The headaches haven't let up all week.
Business won't let up until January.

senses.head: let up on — go easier on
body: Of a person under pressure.
examples: Let up on him — he's been here two days.
The defense never let up on the quarterback.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — the rain let UP
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object; the person you go easier on follows on, as in let up on the kid.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes a direct object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of a process weakening; the subject is usually weather, pain, or pressure rather than a person. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — it takes no direct object, and the prepositional passive of let up on is not idiomatic: ✗ the quarterback was never let up on, ✗ the rain was let up.
entries.see also: lay off, hold off, leave off

entries.meaning: Be left untidily in the open, or spend time doing nothing. Many Americans say lay around in speech; it is very common and still counted as nonstandard.
examples: There were tools lying around the whole garage.
Don't leave cash lying around.
He lay around the house all weekend.
I'd love a Saturday to just lie around and read.
They lay around the pool until the sun went down.

senses.head: Be left lying about
body: Of objects nobody has put away.
examples: There were tools lying around the whole garage.
Don't leave cash lying around.

senses.head: Do nothing
body: Of people, usually with a note of disapproval.
examples: He lay around the house all weekend.
I'd love a Saturday to just lie around and read.
They lay around the pool until the sun went down.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lie aROUND all day
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object; this lie never takes one. Careful: the transitive verb is lay, so a person lies around but lays the tools around.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 2 (a person doing nothing all weekend); sense 1, of objects left out, is closer to stative — it reports where things are, like locative be, and tools were lying around names a state, not an event.
entries.passive: no — this lie never takes an object at all (the transitive verb is lay), so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the garage was lain around. Contrast the genuine passive of the transitive verb: the tools were laid around the garage.
entries.see also: lie low, hang around, lay down

entries.meaning: Be the hidden reason or cause of something.
examples: Nobody has explained what lies behind the sudden closure.
A long grudge lay behind the lawsuit.
The economics that lie behind the policy are never discussed.
Fear, not principle, lay behind the vote.
There's a longer story lying behind that photograph.
entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — what LIES behind it; behind is a preposition and keeps its object
entries.separable: no — the object always follows behind. What lies behind the decision, ✗ what lies the decision behind; with a pronoun, what lies behind it, ✗ what lies it behind.
entries.verb type: stative — a relation of cause that simply holds; nobody performs it. It resists the progressive except as a stylistic flourish (a longer story is lying behind that photograph is odd; lies behind is what you write).
entries.passive: no — ✗ the decision is lain behind by a grudge, ✗ the closure was lain behind. Note too that the participle of this lie is lain, which never appears in a passive at all; use was caused by or was driven by.

entries.meaning: Stay in bed later than usual in the morning.
examples: On Sundays they lie in until ten.
I was hoping to lie in for once.
She had a long lie-in after the night shift.
An American would not say lie in; he would say he slept in.
Students lie in half the term and then panic in May.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — have a lie-IN
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object to move.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.register: British — Americans say sleep in; the British noun lie-in is an American sleep-in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of staying in bed deliberately. British; the American equivalent is sleep in. The noun lie-in comes from it.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, with no object to promote: ✗ Sunday was lain in. Only the noun is available: she had a long lie-in.

entries.meaning: Stay out of sight and avoid attention until trouble passes. Americans very often say lay low, which is nonstandard but everywhere.
examples: He lay low for a month after the story broke.
Lie low until the auditors are finished.
The suspects were lying low somewhere in the valley.
After the argument she lay low and let him cool off.
In American speech you will hear lay low far more often than lie low.
entries.pronunciation note: the second word takes the stress — lie LOW
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object to move.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic as a course of behavior (he lay low for a month), but grammatically lie here is linking: low is an adjective complement describing the subject, exactly as in lie still or lie quiet, not an object or a particle.
entries.passive: no — there is no object, and a complement can never become a passive subject: ✗ low was lain, ✗ he was lain low in this sense. (He was laid low by the flu is a different verb, transitive lay.)

entries.meaning: Be the responsibility or the choice of a particular person or body.
examples: The final decision lies with the board.
Responsibility for the delay lies with the contractor.
The choice lies with you and nobody else.
Whatever fault there is lies with me.
He shall not lie with his neighbor's wife.

senses.head: Be the responsibility of
body: Of decisions, blame, and duties. The subject is the decision, not the person.
examples: The final decision lies with the board.
Responsibility for the delay lies with the contractor.
The choice lies with you and nobody else.
Whatever fault there is lies with me.

senses.head: Have sex with
body: Archaic and biblical; you meet it only in older translations.
examples: He shall not lie with his neighbor's wife.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — the decision LIES with the board
entries.separable: no — the object always follows with. The choice lies with you, ✗ the choice lies you with; with a pronoun, it lies with them, ✗ it lies them with.
entries.verb type: stative — a relation of responsibility that holds rather than happens; the subject is the decision or the blame, never an agent. It resists the progressive: ✗ the decision is lying with the board.
entries.passive: no — stative and prepositional, so the object cannot be promoted: ✗ the board is lain with by the decision, ✗ the contractor is lain with. Recast as the board decides or the contractor is responsible. The archaic sense 2 has no passive either.

entries.meaning: Come upon something by chance, or settle on it as a bird does.
examples: She lit on the answer while doing the dishes.
He lit upon the letter in a box of his father's papers.
The committee finally lit on a name everyone could live with.
A cardinal lit on the feeder.
Her eye lit on the one photograph she hadn't seen.

senses.head: Come upon by chance
body: Of an idea, a phrase, a piece of evidence.
examples: She lit on the answer while doing the dishes.
He lit upon the letter in a box of his father's papers.
The committee finally lit on a name everyone could live with.

senses.head: Settle, come to rest
body: Of a bird, an insect, or a gaze.
examples: A cardinal lit on the feeder.
Her eye lit on the one photograph she hadn't seen.

entries.pronunciation note: verb-stressed — she LIT on the answer; on is a preposition here
entries.русский: наткнуться на, набрести на; сесть (о птице)
entries.separable: no — the object always follows on. She lit on a solution, ✗ she lit a solution on; with a pronoun, he lit on it, ✗ he lit it on.
entries.register: formal — literary; light upon is the same verb and even more bookish
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and punctual in both senses: the instant of stumbling on an idea, or a bird's touching down.
entries.passive: restricted, and in practice avoided — ?the answer was lit on while she did the dishes, ?a name was finally lit on. This is a literary verb that stays in the active; use was hit upon or was settled on if you need a passive.

entries.meaning: Leave in a hurry, usually for somewhere far away.
examples: He lit out for California the week he turned eighteen.
They lit out before the sheriff got there.
Huck Finn decides to light out for the Territory.
She lit out of that town and never wrote.
Every spring he threatens to light out and buy a boat.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — light OUT for the coast
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object; the destination follows for.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes an object
entries.register: rare — dated and distinctly American; informal in tone, and you meet it most in older fiction
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a sudden departure. Intransitive; no stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — it takes no object, and the destination sits in a for-phrase: ✗ California was lit out for, ✗ the town was lit out of.

entries.meaning: Make something bright, become bright with feeling, or start smoking. American English prefers the past lit.
examples: Floodlights lit up the whole field.
One candle lit the room up more than you'd expect.
It's a dark hallway — light it up.
Her face lit up when she saw the dog.
The kids lit up at the word snow.
He lit up the moment he got outside.
The rookie lit up the Celtics for forty points.

senses.head: Illuminate
body: Separable.
examples: Floodlights lit up the whole field.
One candle lit the room up more than you'd expect.
It's a dark hallway — light it up.

senses.head: Become bright with feeling
body: No object, of a face or eyes.
examples: Her face lit up when she saw the dog.
The kids lit up at the word snow.

senses.head: Start smoking
body: Informal, usually with no object.
examples: He lit up the moment he got outside.

senses.head: Dominate an opponent
body: American sports slang.
examples: The rookie lit up the Celtics for forty points.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — light it UP
entries.separable: yes — light up the room or light the room up, and with a pronoun it must split: light it up, never ✗ light up it. In the "face brightens" sense there is no object.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you illuminate something, none when a face brightens or a smoker lights up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense. Sense 2 is inchoative and intransitive — a face becomes bright — which is a change of state, not a linking use: her face lit up, not ✗ her face lit up bright.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the whole field was lit up by floodlights, the Celtics were lit up for forty points. No passive of senses 2 and 3: ✗ her face was lit up when she saw the dog as a passive (that is the adjective), ✗ a cigarette was lit up by him is stiff for he lit up.

entries.meaning: End up without the benefit that others get.
examples: Somebody always loses out when the rules change midstream.
Renters lost out badly in that reform.
If you don't file by Friday, you lose out.
She lost out twice before finally getting the promotion.
The small farms lose out every single time.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — lose OUT, never LOSE out
entries.separable: n/a — there is no object; what you miss follows on and who beat you follows to.
entries.transitive: no — it never takes a direct object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of ending up worse off than others. Intransitive; no stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — it takes no direct object at all, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the reform was lost out by renters, ✗ the promotion was lost out.
entries.see also: lose out on, lose out to

entries.meaning: Miss a chance to get something worth having.
examples: By waiting a week she lost out on the lower rate.
Don't lose out on the match just because the form is annoying.
They lost out on the house by four thousand dollars.
He lost out on years with his kids for a job he later quit.
The bonus closes tonight — I'm not going to lose out on it.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle carries the stress — lose OUT on it
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Lose out on the bonus, ✗ lose the bonus out on; with a pronoun, lose out on it, ✗ lose it out on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of missing a chance; the subject is the person who misses it, and what is missed follows on.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive is not idiomatic: ✗ the lower rate was lost out on, ✗ the house was lost out on by four thousand dollars. Recast as she missed out on the lower rate or the plain the bonus was missed.
entries.see also: lose out, lose out to, leave out

entries.meaning: Be beaten to something by a rival.
examples: She lost out to an internal candidate.
The town lost out to Louisville for the plant.
Independent stores keep losing out to the warehouse chains.
Our bid lost out to one that came in a day earlier.
They were the favorites and still lost out to a team nobody had heard of.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle particle carries the stress — lose OUT to them
entries.separable: no — three-part verbs never split. Lose out to a rival, ✗ lose a rival out to; with a pronoun, lose out to them, ✗ lose them out to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of being beaten to something by a rival. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — ✗ an internal candidate was lost out to, ✗ Louisville was lost out to by the town. The idiomatic passive belongs to the rival's verb instead: she was beaten out by an internal candidate.
entries.see also: lose out, lose out on, keep up with
